Let a repeated short answer carry the claim when the strength of the case is its consistency.
Bookend the cards in black

Slide 0 and Slide 14 are white type on black, while every comparison card between them is black type on off-white.
The colour switch may signal the start and end of a long carousel without page numbers.
Use an inverted colour scheme for the opening and closing frames of a long repeated series.

DcmS30MjxKF.headline: Show the newspaper ad in readers’ hands across parks and transit
DcmS30MjxKF.summary: Handheld photos put the two-page spread on a bench, against brick, in front of a reader’s face and on a commuter’s lap. The ad’s light-versus-dark page split stays the recurring image while the settings change.

decisions: Show the spread in real hands
Hands, laps and a bench show the ad as a printed object people actually held.
Slide 2 shows two hands pressing the spread flat against brick, and Slide 4 shows a seated reader holding it open in front of her face.
Physical context may make a print buy feel real and public rather than a mock-up.
When promoting offline media, photograph it in use instead of posting the flat artwork.
Contrast the two pages
The white page and the grey page carry the same headline, so the split itself makes the comparison.
On Slides 0, 2 and 4 the left page is white with dark type and the right page is dark grey with white type under an identical headline.
The tonal split may read as a before-and-after even where the numbered lists are too fine to read.
Let a layout’s light-dark division express a comparison when its detailed copy will be seen small.
Vary the setting
Each frame moves the paper to a different place in the city.
The sequence moves from a park bench to grass, a brick wall, a park lawn, a bench reader and a transit seat with red chairs.
Changing locations could suggest the ad was widely encountered, though the frames show only a few readers.
Show one printed piece in several everyday settings to signal reach without stating numbers.

Dcd7GqIuPm_.headline: Pose the career dilemma as a question, then let two curves answer
Dcd7GqIuPm_.summary: Two labelled curves start together near age 22 and fan apart, with each worker’s raise rule written beside its endpoint. The headline question is answered by the gap at 65 rather than by a stated figure.
Dcd7GqIuPm_.formula: Familiar question → Equal starting salary → Two diverging curves → Endpoint labels with raise rules
decisions: Label lines at their endpoints
Names and raise rules sit beside each curve’s final dot, so no separate legend is needed.
Job Switcher: and Job Stayer: labels with their raise rules sit at the right ends of the lime and pink curves.
Direct labels may let readers connect each assumption to its outcome without looking away from the lines.
Put series labels where the lines finish instead of in a separate legend.
Open with a familiar question
A conversational question frames a financial projection as a personal choice.
Should I stay or should I go? heads the slide in large white type above a one-paragraph explanation.
A question the reader may already be asking could draw them into a chart they might otherwise skip.
Headline a projection with the decision it informs, phrased as the reader would ask it.
Start both series at one point
A shared origin makes the gap entirely the result of the different raise rules.
Both curves leave the same point near age 22 and $0, and the dek says both workers start out earning $60,000/year.
An identical start could make the comparison feel fair and the divergence easier to attribute.
When comparing scenarios, hold the starting conditions equal and say so in the copy.

DavMssAOOsk.headline: Chart daytime against overnight returns for nine stocks as paired pills
DavMssAOOsk.summary: A dumbbell chart joins a green daytime pill and a blue overnight pill for each stock on one line. A spooky question headline introduces the overnight drift pattern.
DavMssAOOsk.formula: Spooky question → Two-colour legend → Paired returns per stock → Sources and disclaimer
decisions: Pair two values on one line per row
Each stock’s two returns sit at the ends of one bar, so the gap carries the story.
Nine rows run from Tesla to Him & Her Health, each joining a green daytime pill to a blue overnight pill along an olive line.
The length of each line may make the overnight gap visible before any number is read.
Use a dumbbell layout when the difference between two measures matters more than either value.
Print the value inside each marker
Labels in the pills remove the need to read the axis.
Each pill holds its own figure, such as -14% and 2,945% for GameStop, in white text on green or blue.
Readers may compare exact values without tracing gridlines.
Put the number inside the data mark when readers need exact values at a glance.
Frame the data with a playful question
A spooky idiom turns a market anomaly into a hook.
The headline asks “What goes bump in the night?” and answers “Stock prices” on its second line.
The question and answer may draw in readers who would skip a technical title.
Borrow a familiar phrase that maps onto the data’s surprising pattern.
